samples.text:
Nowadays, false information, or fake news, can spread very fast on social media. This situation causes many problems for people and society. In this essay I will explain these problems and suggest some ways to reduce it.

The first problem is that people can make wrong decisions. For example, during a health crisis, some people read false information online about medicines and they believe it, so they do not follow the advice of doctors. This can be very dangerous for their health. Another problem is that fake news can make people angry with each other. Sometimes a false story about a group of people or a politician is shared thousands of times, and people start to hate each other without knowing the true. As a result, the society become more divided. Also, when there is so much false information, people do not know what to believe and they stop trusting even the real news.

There are some ways to solve this problem. Firstly, social media companies should check the posts more carefully and remove false information quickly. They can use technology and also employ more people to do this job. Secondly, schools should teach students how to check if information is true or not, for example by looking at the source and comparing it with other websites. Thirdly, people themselves need to be responsible. Before they share something, they should think carefully if it is true or it is only a rumour.

In conclusion, false information on social media can cause dangerous decisions, conflict and lack of trust. I believe that social media companies, schools and users must work together to stop the spreading of fake news.
samples.why: Addresses both problems and solutions · relevant points with simple examples and limited depth · clear but mechanical organisation · adequate vocabulary · several errors in word form, pronoun reference and articles.

samples.text:
The rise of social media has transformed the way news is shared, but it has also allowed false information to reach millions of people within hours. This essay will examine the problems this causes and suggest several measures that could limit the spread of misleading content.

One serious problem is the risk to public health and safety. When false claims about medical treatments or vaccines circulate widely, some people may ignore professional advice and make decisions that endanger themselves and others. False information can also damage social harmony. Rumours that target particular communities or individuals can provoke anger and, in extreme cases, violence, while misleading political content can influence how people vote. Perhaps most worrying in the long term is the loss of trust. When people are constantly exposed to contradictory claims, they may begin to doubt all sources of information, including reliable journalism and official advice, which makes it harder for societies to respond to real crises.

Reducing the spread of false information requires a combination of approaches. Social media platforms have a clear responsibility, and they should invest more in detecting and labelling misleading posts, as well as reducing the visibility of accounts that repeatedly share false content. However, platforms cannot solve the problem on their own. Education is perhaps the most sustainable solution, and schools should teach media literacy so that young people learn to question sources, check facts and recognise manipulated images. Independent fact-checking organisations also play an important role and deserves greater support. Finally, individuals should develop the habit of pausing before sharing content, particularly when it provokes a strong emotional reaction.

In conclusion, false information on social media endangers health, divides communities and undermines trust. Responsible platforms, media literacy education and careful individual behaviour are all needed to reduce its spread.
samples.why: Clear position throughout · three problems extended with consequences · solutions balanced across platforms, schools and users · good cohesion and collocation (social harmony, media literacy) · one minor agreement slip.

samples.text:
Social media has made it possible for a rumour posted in one country to reach millions of screens worldwide before any journalist has had the chance to verify it. The speed and scale at which falsehoods now travel create problems that go well beyond individual misunderstanding, and tackling them requires action on several fronts.

The most immediate danger concerns decisions that affect health and safety. False claims about miracle cures or the risks of established treatments can lead people to reject sound medical advice, with consequences not only for themselves but for those around them. Misinformation also has a corrosive effect on social cohesion. Fabricated stories that scapegoat minority groups can inflame hostility, and online rumours have at times been followed by real-world violence. In the political sphere, deliberately misleading content can distort public debate and undermine confidence in elections. Underlying all of these is a gradual erosion of trust: when accurate and inaccurate information circulate side by side, many people become cynical about every source, making it harder for legitimate institutions to communicate during genuine emergencies.

Since the problem stems partly from how platforms are designed, the companies behind them must bear much of the responsibility. Algorithms that reward engagement tend to amplify sensational content, so platforms should adjust them to reduce the reach of material flagged as false and invest in faster moderation. Transparent labelling, linking disputed claims to reliable sources, can also help users judge what they read. Regulation may be needed to ensure these commitments are honoured, though it must be carefully framed to avoid restricting legitimate expression. In the longer term, the most durable defence is a public able to evaluate information critically. Media literacy should be embedded in school curricula, teaching students to check sources, recognise manipulated images and notice when content is designed to provoke outrage.

In conclusion, misinformation threatens health, social cohesion and trust in institutions. Better platform design, careful regulation and widespread media literacy together offer the most effective response.
samples.why: Both parts fully addressed with extended, well-reasoned ideas · solutions linked to the causes of spread and qualified sensibly · skilful cohesion · precise vocabulary (corrosive, scapegoat, amplify) · wide range of accurate structures.
